analysis: The broad option retains programming, data and machine learning, adds C++ and Haskell software construction and code review, and connects technical work to database authorisation, organisational strategy, user research and iterative product design. Empirical and qualitative methods complement user and organisational evidence. Ethics remains through AI Ethics; software development is a better fit than a second general ethics course in this option. The data option retains all selections and develops a dedicated linear algebra, probability, numerical methods and systems-modelling sequence feeding machine learning, search and evaluated predictive models, with organisational interpretation and ethics. The human option cannot keep all original courses under current offerings. Psycholinguistics has only an early spring placement after the gateway and the full plan is infeasible even with compensating moves. Advanced Research Methods & Statistics instead adds systematic review, bias assessment and meta-analysis, a stronger continuation of experimental methods for evaluating evidence about people. It sits after the gateway and introductory empirical methods. Retained cognition, perception, social psychology, persuasion and product design support user-centred work. Civil society and institutional trust supply a social context rather than technical design content. The options differ pairwise by five, seven and ten courses (37.5, 52.5 and 75 EC). All three sustain the organising interests. Product design and perception are bounded contributions, not UX-engineering training. Software development supports a partial development-methods correspondence while digital-ecosystem architecture, business-process modelling and information security remain dedicated Utrecht study. The closest and human options each include business evidence through market and organisational research, avoiding a claim of technical AI methods for the nontechnical AI business course.

alignment.rationale: Both develop computational thinking through Python programming.
Both connect the organisation of data to relational databases. UCR covers SQL, normalisation and query processing.
Utrecht brings human communication, visual information and computer-mediated exchange into one course. UCR approaches these areas across courses.
Utrecht has a dedicated course in modelling organisational processes.
Both develop approaches to designing and building software. Utrecht focuses on methods for developing information systems. UCR includes programming, testing and code review.
Utrecht studies how digital services and organisations fit together in an ecosystem.
Utrecht has a dedicated product software course covering the technical and commercial sides of software products.
Utrecht has a dedicated information security course. UCR covers related topics in database authorisation and AI ethics.
Both study organisations and their needs. UCR introduces entrepreneurship and core business functions. Utrecht focuses on how organisations use ICT.
Both examine how organisations use digital technology to pursue strategic goals.
Both use research into user needs to guide design. UCR prototypes consumer products. Utrecht focuses on interactive digital systems.
UCR introduces the brain and behaviour, including foundations for studying cognition. Utrecht has a dedicated course on cognition and emotion.
UCR studies how people perceive and act. Utrecht teaches how to design and evaluate usable digital systems.
Utrecht combines people, society and ICT in one course. UCR studies aspects of that relationship through sociology, business and AI ethics.
Both develop empirical research design and analysis.
UCR develops argument and communication through rhetoric. Utrecht develops academic skills for information science.
Utrecht requires an individual 15 EC project after 120 EC and Scientific Research Methods. UCR’s optional independent research is separate from the scheduled courses.
Utrecht students choose 45 EC of profiling electives, including at least 15 EC at intermediate or advanced level. Choices must avoid overlap with other courses.
